10251-town-geology:
These Victorian lectures explain geology for town readers who may never visit a quarry or a cliff. The writer starts with the soil under a field, then builds outward to rocks, strata, and the long ages that shaped them. His image is simple: geology studies the rind of the earth, while astronomy asks what lies inside.

Later talks show how hills, valleys, coasts, and city ground were made and worn away. The style is friendly and full of homely comparisons, aimed at curious minds rather than experts. Readers get a clear, old-style introduction to how the ground beneath a town came to be.
13205-civics-as-applied-sociology:
Patrick Geddes's Civics as Applied Sociology, read before the Sociological Society on July 18, 1904, with Charles Booth in the chair, argues that cities must be surveyed before they can be governed. Geddes begins with London, vast and foggy, and asks where a civic survey should start. He praises Booth's social survey, yet notes even London remains a labyrinth.

Geddes holds that civics is the joint life of a city, too much for one man to hold, and that each town must work out its own scheme. He cites Rowntree's work in York, done with his advice, as a model of local study. Tradition, he adds, is to a community what memory is to a person. The paper is a founding text of town planning as social science.
15076-some-principles-of-maritime-strate:
Julian S. Corbett's 1911 work Some Principles of Maritime Strategy sets out theory of war, natures of wars offensive and defensive, limited and unlimited, limited war and maritime empires, and wars of intervention. Conditions of strength in limited war follow.

Theory of the object, command of the sea, theory of means, constitution of fleets, and theory of method, concentration and dispersal of force, complete the first part. Methods of securing, disputing and exercising command follow. Corbett writes for naval officers and students, arguing sea power is about command, not merely battle. The book shaped British naval thought before the First World War.
15120-the-broadway-anthology:
Four New York writers of 1917 join forces in this anthology of Broadway life, with Edward Bernays, Samuel Hoffenstein, Walter Kingsley, and Murdock Pemberton each taking a section. Poems and short prose pieces cover press agents, chorus men, prima donnas, and first nights. The book first ran in New York papers and magazines.

Bernays writes of accidents, photographs, and the distribution of credit, while Hoffenstein turns to scrubwomen, jesters, and cabaret singers. Kingsley sketches George M. Cohan and David Belasco, and Pemberton closes with Pavlova and night-time Broadway. Together they give a lively, insider portrait of the stage world just before America entered the war.
16136-american-addresses-with-a-lecture-:
Thomas H. Huxley's American Addresses, published in London by Macmillan in 1877, gathers his 1876 visit to the United States. Three New York lectures on evolution open the book, testing the hypotheses of nature's history, the neutral and favorable evidence, and the demonstrative evidence for evolution. An address at the opening of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore follows, with a lecture on studying biology at South Kensington.

Huxley, Darwin's great defender, argues with clarity, wit, and a teacher's patience. The volume shows Victorian science speaking to a new American audience at a hopeful moment. Students of evolution, education, and science writing will find it a landmark collection.
1656-apology:
In Athens in 399 BC, an old man stood before a jury of his fellow citizens. He faced two charges: that he did not believe in the city's gods, and that he corrupted the young. Charged with impiety and with corrupting the young, Socrates answers by describing his life. He cites the oracle's claim that no man was wiser, his habit of questioning statesmen, poets, and craftsmen, and his refusal to flatter the jury.

The speech ends with his conviction and death sentence, and with Socrates still insisting that a good man cannot be harmed by an unjust verdict. Readers meet the philosopher at his most direct, arguing that knowing one's ignorance is worth more than reputation, and that he would rather die than stop asking questions.
17229-the-haunted-hour-an-anthology:
Margaret Widdemer's 1920 anthology, The Haunted Hour, gathers poems of ghosts, All Souls, and the night between saints and souls. Contents run from Katherine Tynan's All-Souls and Lizette Reese's All-Saints' Eve to George Macdonald's Janet's Tryst, Marjorie Pickthall's Mary Shepherdess, and Yeats's folk of the air. Permissions from Doran, Dutton, Harper, Holt, and Macmillan fill the copyright page.

Widdemer groups poems by mood: sighing souls, little dead children, and purgatory's open door. The set suits readers who like ghost verse that is tender as well as eerie. It is a fine Halloween shelf book, where classic and modern poets meet in the haunted hour.
17280-anthropology:
R. R. Marett's Anthropology, number 37 in the Home University Library, surveys the science of man in ten chapters. Scope, antiquity of man, race, environment, language, social organization, law, religion, morality, and man the individual run from page 7 to 241, with a bibliography and index. Marett, reader in social anthropology at Oxford, opens with prehistoric brothers born and died in darkness, yet rescuing the torch of life for us.

His prose is clear, humane, and general, made for readers new to the field. The book suits students who want a short, classic map of anthropology's questions. As a period survey, it shows early twentieth-century science at work, and should be read with its age in mind.
18188-homer-and-classical-philology:
Friedrich Nietzsche gave Homer and Classical Philology as his inaugural address at Basel University on May 28, 1869, printed here from his collected works, translated by J. M. Kennedy. Nietzsche, then a young professor, asks what classical philology truly is.

He finds no clear, agreed view of the field, since it mixes history, science, and art under one name, like a magic potion of odd liquors, ores, and bones. Yet it holds an artistic, moral force that lifts it past mere learning. The address is short, bold, and early Nietzsche, a fine start for readers who want his mind before the great books.
18911-biology:
Edmund Beecher Wilson, professor of zoology at Columbia, delivered this lecture on biology at the university on November 20, 1907, published by the Columbia University Press in 1908. Wilson warns at the outset that no single science owns the name biology, which covers a whole group of sciences of life.

The biologist's double task, he says, is to resolve the living organism into simpler factors, through morphology and physiology, and to study it as a product of history. Darwin, more than any other, brought home that present life is the outcome of evolution, and that morphology and physiology are inseparable. The lecture serves as a preface to fuller talks on physiology, botany, and zoology.
19019-aids-to-forensic-medicine-and-toxi:
W. G. Aitchison Robertson, a lecturer in Edinburgh, wrote this 1922 handbook of forensic medicine and toxicology in its ninth edition. It guides doctors who must give evidence, examine the dead, and judge sudden death, poisoning, and crime. The book is meant for students and working practitioners alike.

Chapters cover personal identity, signs of death, coroners' inquests, and the care a medical witness must take with his sworn words. Fees, statutes, and court practice are set out in plain terms. Readers get a clear, practical aid to law and medicine, firm on duty and detail.
19499-music-notation-and-terminology:
Karl W. Gehrkens wrote this guide to music notation and terms, published in the mid nineteen teens. Chapters define symbols, abbreviations, signs, and embellishments, then move through scales, measure, tempo, and the words that tell players how a piece should sound.

A section on recitative explains speech-like song, once backed by a single cello line, with full chords shown only by signs and figures. The book, with audio in its online form, remains a clear primer for students learning to read music. A chapter on embellishments teaches the trill, the mordent, and the turn, each with its own sign.
19518-siouan-sociology:
James Owen Dorsey wrote this posthumous paper on Siouan sociology, printed in the Smithsonian's annual report for the mid eighteen nineties. Dorsey, sent to Dakota as a missionary in his early twenties, won Native trust by his ear for language and spent two years learning Ponka and kindred dialects.

The paper maps tribal groups, from the Kwapa villages known to French explorers to clans named for taboos such as not touching a buffalo calf. It remains a careful record of Siouan kinship and social order, built on fieldwork rather than guesswork.
21099-more-about-peggy:
Mrs G. de Horne Vaizey continues the story of Peggy in this sequel from the end of the nineteenth century. Its world already has electricity, telephones, trains, and buses, though middle-class homes still run on servants. The book opens at sea, on a P and O steamer crossing the Bay of Bengal toward England in bright sun.

Peggy's feelings and friendships carry the story more than big events do. Vaizey was known for girls' fiction that took young women's inner lives seriously. Snow in England waits at the end of the voyage home. Readers of the first Peggy book get the same warm, observant manner here.
22668-poems-of-to-day-an-anthology:
Poems of To-Day is an anthology of modern English verse, gathered for schools and general readers in the years of the Great War. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. Its preface explains the plan: a gathering meant to show what living poets made of history, faith, and daily duty.

The poems fall into three groups, the editor says, beginning with poems of history and of England's own tradition and the duties that tradition lays on its heirs. Some poems come straight from the present war, yet the editor hopes nothing here will shame the book in happier days. Such anthologies carried new poets into classrooms by the thousand. This one preserves the taste of its moment: earnest, patriotic, and hungry for beauty under fire.
22748-explanation-of-terms-used-in-entom:
Explanation of Terms Used in Entomology is a glossary of the technical language of insect science, prepared for an entomological society's new edition. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Every science builds a vocabulary of hard words, and entomology's, drawn from Latin and Greek, needed a standard key.

The preface tells how the work grew: the society voted for a new edition and gave the writer two associates to prepare it. They expected a light summer job of dropping obsolete terms and adding a few new ones, with a report due in fall. It proved larger, as glossaries do. The book still serves historians of science, and any reader who has wondered what entomologists mean by their harder words.
2378-select-epigrams-from-the-greek-anth:
J. W. Mackail selects epigrams from the Greek Anthology, the great collection of short poems spanning the ancient world. Select Epigrams offers love poems, epitaphs, dedications, and jokes, translated with grace and brevity. Mackail's choices favor wit and feeling over obscurity, making the ancient voices feel near.

The epigrams range from tender to biting, often within a few lines. The volume serves as an ideal introduction to Greek lyric in miniature. Poetry lovers will find a book to dip into again and again. Mackail also translated Virgil and wrote a life of William Morris.
24456-fathers-of-biology:
Charles McRae, formerly a scholar of Exeter College, Oxford, published this book in London in 1890. It tells the lives of five great naturalists. Each one, McRae argues, pushed biology forward in a distinct way. The book aims to show students that the facts of anatomy and physiology were not all found by recent workers.

Through biography, McRae traces how each naturalist observed, experimented, and reasoned. Their work built the knowledge later generations took for granted. The book suits readers who want the human story behind biology: curious, hard-working observers whose discoveries still shape how the science is taught.
25448-peggy:
Laura E. Richards writes of New England village life in this story of Peggy and her circle. A Boston Post notice praises her delicate treatment of village character, and the front matter recalls Captain January and Melody. The tale follows young people through courtship, weddings, and family feeling, with humour and warmth.

Its wedding scene comes through Gertrude's eager retelling, as Roger and his bride speak clearly at the altar and the music breaks out. Jerry and the colonel nearly break down, and the colonel's nose-blowing makes Jerry wince. Gertrude, once nicknamed Chelsea Waterworks for her tears, has nearly outgrown her childish weeping. The book belongs to Richards' Margaret books.
25601-fasting-girls-their-physiology-and:
William A. Hammond, professor of diseases of the mind and nervous system in New York and Vermont, writes this 1879 study of fasting girls, published by Putnam. His epigraphs borrow Ecclesiastes, that there is no new thing under the sun, and Phaedrus, urging ears neither to scorn nor to trust at once.

Hammond, also author of a book on cerebral hyperaemia from mental strain, examines girls famed for living without food, testing claims against physiology and pathology. The study asks what the body can bear, what illness or fraud may explain, and how doctors should judge wonders that draw crowds.
26382-ancient-america-in-notes-on-americ:
John D. Baldwin's Ancient America, issued by Harper and Brothers in 1871, sums up what was then known of American antiquities. Baldwin, author of Pre-Historic Nations, notes that knowledge lay scattered in French, Spanish, and great English quartos, with no single work giving a whole view. His book aims to fill that gap for general readers, covering all time before Columbus.

A gateway at Labna fronts the volume, and later pages follow Lieutenant Whipple west along the thirty-fifth parallel. Ruins show cedar beams, obsidian arrow heads, and painted pottery, with a Pueblo ruin at Pecos among the sights. A paper on Pacific Island antiquities closes the set. The book offers a Victorian survey of mounds, cities, and relics across the Americas.
27500-the-new-theology:
R. J. Campbell, minister of the City Temple in London, published this statement of liberal theology with the Macmillan Company in New York in March 1907, reprinted the next month. Campbell begins by separating religion from theology: religion and theology differ: theology gives intellectual form to religious experience, and no one with a real religious experience can help having one.

Chapters take up God and the universe, man in relation to God, the nature of evil, and the eternal Christ. They go on to the incarnation and the atonement in three parts, covering its association with Jesus, Semitic ideas of atonement, and its place in Christian history and experience. Scripture, salvation and judgment, and the church and kingdom close the book. It stirred wide debate in its day.
27842-the-economic-aspect-of-geology:
C. K. Leith of the University of Wisconsin wrote this 1921 textbook on the economic aspects of geology, published by Henry Holt and Company. It surveys how each branch of geology bears on finding and using mineral deposits.

Chapters cover the common elements, minerals, and rocks of the earth, the classification of deposits, and their formation by igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic processes. Leith wrote for students and prospectors who needed geology as a practical science, linking field observation to mines, ores, and industry. Leith surveys mineralogy, stratigraphy, structural geology, physiography, and metamorphism in his opening chapter.
2935-on-the-study-of-zoology:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote On the Study of Zoology as a defense of natural history, the study of minerals, plants, and animals. He recalls Linnaeus as a naturalist in the wide sense, whose Systema Naturae gathered all that was known of natural bodies in his time. The essay distinguishes the natural sciences from other physical sciences and explains what a naturalist actually does. Huxley brings a lobster to life as his example.

He imagines a reader who knows it only as an inert mass, an organic crystal, and then sees it tear and crush flesh with multitudinous jaws. The new question becomes how all this takes place, and the new idea is adaptation to a way of life. The essay still serves as an invitation to zoology for curious beginners.
3374-the-entire-march-family-trilogy:
William Dean Howells's March family trilogy gathers three novels in one volume. Their Wedding Journey leads, from the outset through a midsummer-day's dream, the night boat, and a day's railroading. The enchanted city and beyond, Niagara, down the St Lawrence, and the sentiment of Montreal follow, with homeward and home, Niagara revisited, and twelve years after their wedding.

A Hazard of New Fortunes, in five parts, forms the middle panel, and Their Silver Wedding Journey, in three volumes, closes the set. Together the three books follow Basil and Isabel March from honeymoon to silver wedding, across a changing America. Readers get Howells's great domestic chronicle whole: one marriage, three journeys, and a nation's manners in between.
3772-the-student-s-elements-of-geology:
Charles Lyell, author of the Principles of Geology, abridged his great work into this student textbook, rich with more than six hundred woodcut illustrations. The book sorts rocks by origin and age, from aqueous strata laid down in water to volcanic, plutonic, and metamorphic forms, and it explains stratification, fossils, and the earth's crust in order. Tertiary, Secondary, and Primary divisions frame the whole story of deep time.

Later chapters read fossils as evidence, with corals, shells, crocodile teeth, and a thirteen foot sea snake from Sheppey pointing to vanished shores. Lyell writes with the calm authority that made him the age's chief geologist. Students of earth science history will find a clear window on Victorian geology, while general readers gain a solid first map of rocks and ages.
4204-the-elements-of-geology:
W. H. Norton's Elements of Geology explains the earth for students, chapter by chapter, from rain to rock. A chapter on rivers and valleys turns from water that soaks into the ground to the run-off that washes along the surface.

Fed by rains and melting snows, the run-off gathers into faint courses that join deeper channels, as twigs join stems. In humid climates, larger ravines carry the flow onward, cutting valleys as they go. Readers who want geology in plain, patient prose will find a clear textbook of land and water.
477-criminal-sociology:
Enrico Ferri, of the Italian school of criminology, argues that crime grows from social and physical causes as much as from individual choice. This preliminary text replaces a lost final version, and Ferri's argument still comes through clearly. Ferri, a student of Lombroso, pushed criminology toward social causes and reform.

Ferri weighs heredity, climate, poverty, and law, and he urges prevention and social reform over punishment alone. The book belongs beside Lombroso in the criminology series, and it shaped how later writers thought about crime. His school argued that punishment alone could not cure crime rooted in poverty and drink.
4928-bulfinch-s-mythology:
Bulfinch's Mythology presents the classic retelling of ancient myth for readers who want the stories behind poetry and art. The religions of Greece and Rome are extinct as worship, the opening argues, but their gods survive in literature and taste, bound to the finest productions of ancient and modern imagination.

The volume gathers the Greek and Roman tales that poets, essayists, and orators constantly allude to, told in plain and entertaining prose. No author is named in the catalog record, though the collection is Bulfinch's standard work. Readers get a single handbook for the myths that underlie so much later writing.
5614-chess-strategy:
Edward Lasker wrote Chess Strategy, translated by J. du Mont, in a second edition dated 1915, as a guide to playing chess well. The book contains 167 diagrams in ASCII line drawings, with a key explaining pieces and colors: rook, knight, bishop, queen, king, and pawn, with black pieces marked one way and white another. Rules and notation come first.

Later sections give hints for beginners, general principles of strategy, the opening, the endgame, and the middle game. Readers get a classic instruction book, clear and systematic, for players who want to think beyond single moves.
5694-the-harvard-classics-volume-38-scie:
Volume thirty-eight of the Harvard Classics gathers landmark papers on physiology, medicine, and the workings of the body. Its opening paper follows an early investigator of the heart. He turned to vivisection because books alone could not show when systole and diastole occur. He found the task arduous and full of difficulty. The volume's scope runs from Hippocrates, whose famous Oath is included, through later experimenters who tested ideas by direct observation.

Readers meet science in the act of learning: hypotheses are stated, animals are examined, and old authority is set against what the eye can see. The papers are demanding but rewarding, since each one shows a method as well as a result. For students of medicine and the history of science, this volume offers primary sources that still explain how modern physiology began to separate fact from received opinion.
9380-a-nonsense-anthology:
Carolyn Wells collected this nonsense anthology in 1910, dedicated to Gelett Burgess, a nonsense lover. Its motto, from William Rolfe, holds that he who cannot play the fool at times lacks sense. The crown jewel is Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky, with slithy toves, mome raths, and the frumious Bandersnatch, slain by a vorpal blade.

Anonymous verse joins the famous pieces, all in praise of gleeful absurdity. Wells arranged the book as a feast, not a lesson. It remains a delightful shelf of nonsense, for children and for grown-ups who still enjoy a good burble.
apology:
Plato gives Socrates' defense speech at his trial in Athens, translated by Benjamin Jowett, with an introduction weighing how close the speech stands to what Socrates really said. Socrates stands accused of corrupting the young and denying the gods. He answers by cross-examining his accuser and telling the story of his life.

He explains the oracle that called him wisest, his testing of politicians, poets, and craftsmen, and the divine sign that guides him. Offered chances to beg, flee, or fall silent, he refuses each one. The speech closes with his calm talk of death as either sleep or a passage to better company. It remains a founding text of philosophy.
b09-melanchthon-apology:
The Apology of the Augsburg Confession is Philipp Melanchthon's defense of his confession, written in 1531. Catholic scholars at Augsburg had drawn up a refutation of the Lutheran articles. Melanchthon answered it point by point, at greater length and with sharper argument than the confession itself.

The Apology presses hardest on how a sinner stands right before God, by faith in Christ alone. It ranges across repentance, good works, the mass, and the saints. Lutherans count it among their core confessional books. The translation here is by F Bente and W H T Dau. Few works show Melanchthon's learning and care for clear teaching so fully.
brief-reflections-relative-to-the-emigra: Brief Reflections relative to the Emigrant French Clergy, by Fanny Burney. The exiled priests. This book preserves that pamphlet. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
bulfinch-s-mythology:
Thomas Bulfinch's Mythology gathers his three books in one complete volume. The Age of Fable retells the myths of Greece, Rome, and the north for general readers. The Age of Chivalry follows King Arthur and the knights of romance. Legends of Charlemagne completes the set with the paladins of France.

The publishers' preface ranks The Age of Fable with Pilgrim's Progress and Robinson Crusoe among books everyone must know. Bulfinch, a Boston bank accountant born in 1796, wrote in his leisure from Harvard studies. He meant mythology as a key to literature and art, not as scholarship. Story follows story, plainly told and lightly moralized. For generations of English-speaking children this was the door into Olympus and Camelot. Its versions still shape how the old tales are remembered, quoted, and retold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-in-li:
Abraham holds a special place in Christian liturgy, and this entry traces his name through the prayers and rites of East and West. Of all Old Testament names used in worship, Abel, Melchisedech, and Abraham gain prominence through their link with sacrifice. That link matters above all in the Roman rite's Canon of the Mass. In the Litany for the Dying only two Old Testament names appear, Abel and Abraham, and Abraham occurs so often that his position stands out.

The entry works through his present uses in the Roman liturgy, from the Martyrology entry for 9 October to the commendation of a departing soul. It calls him patriarch and father of all believers. It also looks back to his name in sacred history and early Christian prayer. Its use even in pagan magical formulas, as Origen testifies, shows how widely the patriarch's name travelled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-african-litur:
The African Liturgy was in use not only in old Roman Africa, with Carthage as capital, but also in Numidia and Mauretania, across northern Africa from Egypt's borders west to the Atlantic. Christianity entered proconsular Africa late in the second century, probably through missionaries from Rome, and spread rapidly through the other provinces. The liturgy's language was Latin, modified by many Africanisms.

Probably the oldest Latin liturgy, it was in use long before Rome changed her official language from Greek to Latin. Studying it may therefore trace the origin and growth of different rites and show one rite's influence on another. Since the African church always depended on Rome and stayed devoted to St. Peter's see, liturgical questions were surely raised and customs possibly adopted each way. Later the African liturgy seems to have influenced Mozarabic and Gallican rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnus-dei-in-:
Agnus Dei in liturgy is the thrice-recited Mass formula of the priest in the Roman rite, except on Good Friday and Holy Saturday. It comes toward the Canon's end, after the prayer Haec commixtio. Having finished that prayer, the priest lays the pall over the chalice, genuflects, rises, and inclines his head profoundly toward the altar. Then he says aloud: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis.

In English: Lamb of God, who takest away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. He repeats the formula unchanged, then a third time substitutes dona nobis pacem, grant us peace, striking his breast thrice. In Requiem Masses the formula instead asks dona eis requiem, grant them rest, and dona eis requiem sempiternam, grant them eternal rest, and the priest does not strike his breast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-in-litu:
In the New Law the altar is the Eucharistic Sacrifice's table, and Mass is never celebrated without an altar or at least an altar stone. Only two exceptions appear in church history: St. Lucian celebrating on his breast in prison in 312, and Theodore of Tyre on his deacons' hands. In ancient basilicas the priest faced the people, the apse holding the altar at the end opposite the entrance.

Early altars were probably wood, like Christ's Last Supper table, a Roman wooden table surviving at the Lateran. A fixed altar joins table, support, and sepulchre, the table a single stone slab cemented to its support. A portable altar is a consecrated stone holding host and chalice base. Primitive forms included the arcosolium, a marble slab over a martyr's grave niche in the catacombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-analogy:
Analogy, a term from philosophy, names both a property of things and a way of reasoning. It is treated in four parts: science, scholastic thought, God, and the mysteries of faith. As a property it means likeness mixed with difference. The likeness may live only in the mind, as between sunlight and the light of the mind. It may also rest on real shared traits, as with organs serving the same use in different creatures.

As reasoning, it argues from known likenesses to further ones. Franklin moved by this path from lightning to electricity, and Cuvier rebuilt whole animals from single bones. Scholastic writers refined it into proportion and proportionality, using health as their model, since food, medicine, and a face can all be called healthy for different reasons. Applied to God, it strips limits from what it finds in creatures, then lifts the perfections that remain higher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anatole-de-be:
A martyr of the French Commune, Anatole de Bengy was born at Bourges on 19 September 1824 and died in Paris on 26 May 1871. After nine years at the Jesuit college of Brugelette he entered the Society of Jesus. He served as chaplain to French troops in the Crimean War, then gave himself to college work until 1870.

When the Franco-Prussian War broke out he again became a chaplain, serving the sick and wounded through the siege of Paris. After the war he returned to teach at Sainte-Genevieve. On 3 April National Guards seized the school and held its Jesuits as hostages of the Commune. De Bengy cheered his companions through the wait for death. On 26 May he was led with two Jesuit companions and some forty other victims to the court at Rue Haxo. There he died joyfully amid the shouts of the Communards.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiochene-li:
The Antioch liturgy family begins with the Apostolic Constitutions, then Greek and Syrian St. James, and other Syrian Anaphoras. The line continues to the Byzantine Rite, Basil's older and Chrysostom's shorter liturgies, and through it to Armenian use. These no longer concern Antioch. The Apostolic Constitutions liturgy is the oldest known complete liturgy form. It is the Antiochene line's first member. The Constitutions are eight books ascribed to St. Clement of Rome. The first six books are an interpolated Didascalia edition.

The Constitutions liturgy moves from Institution words to Anamimnesis, remembrance of suffering, death, resurrection, ascension, and second coming. Then Epiklesis invokes the Spirit to change bread and cup, and a great Intercession follows. The developed St. James liturgy adds Diptychs, anti-Nestorian hymns to Our Lady, the Lord's Prayer, and a Communion where the deacon says only Approach in the fear of the Lord.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiphon-in-g:
Antiphons appear throughout the Greek Liturgy: in the Office, at Mass, at Vespers, and at every canonical Hour. Almost every liturgical function gives them a set place. In antiphonal psalmody, soloists and choir take turns rendering a psalm. Alternate singing entered liturgical worship about the fourth century, after use only in secular gatherings until then.

That does not mean antiphonal chanting was new in the fourth century: the Synagogue already used it, and the Church would hardly have waited so long to take it up. What was new was a more ornate melody. Choir-rendered strophes in antiphon form explain why alternate psalmody is called antiphonal. Hymn writers found endless material in those strophes, so psalm verses slowly gave way to added strophes. Some psalms or psalm groups shrank in this way to three or four verses, and sometimes to a single verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostle-in-li: Apostle, in liturgy, is the name the Greek church gives to the Epistle, or letter reading, of the Divine Liturgy. It is always of apostolic origin and never, as sometimes in the Roman rite, sourced from the Old Testament writings. It is also the book holding the Epistles for each Sunday and feast of the year, from which the reader reads the Epistle of the day. As printed at Constantinople, Athens, and Rome, it adds the antiphons and prokeimena, or introductory verses, for the days of the Greek church year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archaeology:
Archaeology, in this entry, means the official pontifical board founded in the mid-nineteenth century to promote and direct digs in the Roman catacombs and other sites of Christian antiquarian interest. It also safeguards objects found there. Its spur was Giovanni Battista De Rossi, pupil of the archaeologist Father Marchi, who had begun investigating underground Rome with results that promised rich reward.

In a vineyard plot on the Appian Way in 1849 De Rossi found a marble fragment reading in part NELIVS MARTYR, which he recognized as part of Pope Cornelius's tomb inscription. Cornelius, martyred in 253, lay in St. Callixtus's catacomb on the Appian Way, and De Rossi argued the vineyard overlay that catacomb. He urged Pius IX to buy the vineyard for digging, and the pope, hearing the young enthusiast, answered that these were but the dreams of an archaeologist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascetical-the:
Ascetical theology, as a branch of theology, is the scientific exposition of Christian asceticism. Asceticism, from Greek askesis, literally means polishing, smoothing, or refining. Greeks used the word for athletes' exercises, by which dormant bodily powers were developed and the body trained to full natural beauty. They aimed at the laurel wreath given to victors in public games.

Christian life, Christ assures us, is a struggle for the kingdom of heaven. Paul, trained in Greek fashion, pictures that spiritual battle with the Greek pentathlon, the five contests, in 1 Corinthians 9:24. Exercises in this combat develop moral stamina, aiming at Christian perfection. The long article expounds that training: its principles, its stages, and its place beside dogmatic and moral theology in the science of the spiritual life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assemblies-of:
The Assemblies of the French Clergy were five-yearly representative meetings of France's clergy to apportion financial burdens kings laid on the church, and incidentally for other church purposes. They had a financial origin, to which, the article argues, the rise of all deliberative assemblies may be traced. Long before them, the state had imposed on the church its share of public expenses.

French kings, powerful, needy, and at times unscrupulous, could hardly see a wealthy body steadily extending its possessions without drawing on its coffers, or if need be pillaging them. During the Middle Ages Crusades brought frequent levies on church property, and the Saladin Tithe began that pattern. The long article follows assemblies from tax bargaining to a forum where clergy debated money, discipline, and the crown's claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-astrology:
Astrology is the supposed science fixing the stars' influence, above all the five older planets, on human fate, called judicial or mundane astrology, or on weather changes, called natural astrology. It works by fixed rules depending on the stars' controlling positions at the time in question. Judicial astrology, the more important branch of this occult art, based predictions on the planets' places in the twelve houses at a person's birth moment.

The calculations settling those positions meant casting the horoscope, or diagram of the heavens, at nativity. Starting from the point rising at birth, the celestial equator was divided into a dozen equal parts, six above and six beneath the horizon. Circles were drawn through those points and the horizon and meridian crossings. The long article then explains houses, aspects, and the church's judgment on a practice that claimed the stars ruled human lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benefit-of-cl:
Benefit of clergy, the medieval English exemption of clergy from secular courts, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. In Saxon days bishops sat beside sheriffs in local courts, but after the Norman Conquest church courts stood apart from civil ones. The privilege covered all who were tonsured, with shaved crown, and wore clerical dress, including monks and nuns.

Gratian's canon law sums the rule: a cleric was not to be brought before public courts in civil or criminal cases. The entry follows the privilege through its widening, its abuses, and its slow narrowing by English kings. It reads as a compact history of church and crown competing for jurisdiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-chro:
Biblical chronology, the dating of Bible events, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It asks whether the Bible holds a chronology at all, how far its writers aimed at exact dates or round numbers, and how far copyists' errors corrupted its figures. Relations with neighbouring peoples' chronologies form the fourth question.

No single era anchored early Bible history, unlike Rome's founding or the later Seleucid era from 312 BC. The entry works in sections from creation and the Flood through Abraham, Exodus, kings, and exile, weighing rival systems. It is a sober admission that Bible dates often resist a single timeline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biology:
Biology, the science of life and living things, receives a long survey in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. From the Greek words for life and account, it studies structure, origin, growth, function, and surroundings of plants and animals, by observation and experiment. Zoology covers animals, botany covers plants, and anthropology covers humankind's body.

Morphology, the study of form, splits into anatomy of gross structure, histology of tissues, and cytology of cells, the ultimate units of life. Classification, physiology, and development follow. The entry is a map of a young science, written before genetics reshaped it, but clear on its branches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celibacy-of-t:
Celibacy is the giving up of marriage, promised implicitly or explicitly for the sake of perfect chastity, by all who receive Orders in any higher grade. Its character is understood differently in the Eastern and Western Churches. In the West, the bishop warns candidates at ordination of the burden they take on. He tells them they are still free to turn back to the world.

But once they receive the order, they must persevere in God's service and chastity. By stepping forward despite the warning, the candidate binds himself equivalently by a vow of chastity and can no longer contract a valid marriage. The long article traces the history of clerical celibacy in two periods, its course in England, and its present position. It also covers the law in the Oriental Churches, closing with an 1898 Coptic synod at Alexandria requiring celibacy of candidates for higher orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-arc:
An entry on Christian archaeology, the study of ancient Christian monuments as a source for early Christian life. The historian has two sources: literary remains and material monuments, from tomb inscriptions, paintings, and sculptures to churches and small crafted objects. Its aim is to learn the manners and customs of the first Christians from what they made and left behind.

Authorities such as De Rossi and Le Blant close Christian antiquity about the death of Gregory the Great in 604. In Gaul and Germany monuments kept an ancient character a century longer. Scientific study began with the Augustinian Onofrio Panvinio in 1554 and 1568, and the chance discovery of a Christian cemetery on the Via Salaria in 1578 opened the field. The entry surveys inscriptions, frescoes, mosaics, basilicas, and minor arts, including textiles, vessels, coins, and miniatures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christology:
An entry on Christology, the part of theology that deals with Our Lord Jesus Christ. In full it covers both His person and His works, but this article limits itself to His person. The historian's and Old Testament scholar's shares go to the articles on Jesus Christ and the Messiah. Its subject is the person of Christ as the New Testament and Christian tradition present Him.

That person is the Second Person of the Trinity, the Son or Word of the Father, incarnate by the Holy Ghost of the Virgin Mary and made man. Foretold in the Old Testament and fully revealed in the New, these mysteries are studied under three aspects: Old Testament, New Testament, and Christian tradition. The Old Testament section notes how Christ and the apostles appealed to messianic prophecies, and how the Fathers prepared a deeper reading of their historical sweep.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commemoration:
Patrick Morrisroe's entry defines a commemoration in liturgy as part of an Office or Mass said for a feast or day when the whole cannot be said. Two Offices may fall on one day, and rubrics may bar moving one to another day. Then the lesser is kept in part, by way of commemoration. Offices carry grades of rank, such as doubles and semi-doubles, fixed at their founding. Rank mainly settles which Office wins when they clash.

At Mass a commemoration means saying the collect, Secret, and Post-Communion proper to the feast remembered. In the Office, commemorations fall at Lauds and Vespers, with antiphons, versicles, and responses of the Benedictus and Magnificat, plus an oremus. Special commemorations differ from common ones, which belong to Offices of lower rite. When two Offices meet, the clash is called occurrence, or concurrence at Vespers, and rank fixes their order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-convocation-o:
Edward Myers's entry defines Convocation, the Church of England's name for what resembles a provincial synod yet differs widely. Canterbury and York each possess one, Canterbury's the more important. Its outward form's history runs on, bound up with English history. Power and freedom vanished at the Reformation, though the body, long a mere form, now voices priestly views. It exercises influence, but holds no power, Crown power remaining supreme.

Its history divides into five periods: before 1295; 1295 to the Reformation; the Reformation period; the post-Reformation period; and modern times. Before 1295 synods regulated discipline. After 1295 beneficed clergy sat in Parliament, and Convocation's link to these men stays obscure. Its Houses split in time, not on Parliament's model. The Act of Submission cost its freedom and powers. Nineteenth-century churchmen revived its use, and the Crown may submit business.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmology:
Cosmology, from Greek words for world and knowledge, names the philosophical science of the material universe. Once broad enough to cover plants, animals, and humanity, the field has narrowed to the world studied apart from the natural sciences. Physics and biology chase proximate causes; cosmology asks after deeper ones.

Three questions organise the entry: the first cause of the world, its constituent causes, and its final purpose. Monism, emanation, and creation face off on origins, while mechanism, dynamism, and the Scholastic hylomorphism debate what matter is made of. Geology, the author notes, always stops at a fact still calling for explanation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demonology:
A wide survey of beliefs about demons across many peoples and ages. Assyrian and Akkadian systems come first, then Iranian, Jewish, early Christian, and medieval and modern forms. True Catholic teaching on fallen angels is set apart from the false and risky systems that fill most of the literature.

Cuneiform records show how old such beliefs are, while Jewish Scripture keeps demon lore spare beside Persian and Assyrian abundance. Early Christian writers faced a crowded field of rival doctrines, and later ages kept borrowing from one system to another. Shared threads run through them all, from belief in evil spirits to modern spiritism, and the closing pages weigh rival explanations for that spread.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divorce-in-mo:
Divorce in moral theology takes up the word where the civil article leaves it. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that pagan Rome used divorce for the mutual parting of spouses. The word alone does not say whether the marriage bond itself was broken. Church law therefore keeps the word neutral and splits it into two kinds.

Absolute divorce dissolves the bond itself, while limited divorce leaves the bond whole and ends only common life. Limited divorce may mean parting from bed and board, or parting of dwelling as well. The entry then sets out the moral teaching in full, with Jewish divorce law and the Christian law of marriage treated side by side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dogmatic-theo:
Dogmatic theology treats the theoretical truths of faith about God and his works, while moral theology treats the practical truths of conduct. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that apologetics was once called general dogmatic theology, though it now stands as its own science and doorway to the field. The article takes up first the basic questions of the science, then its history.

That history follows the acumen and tireless labor of theologians from the fathers through the schoolmen to modern writers. It names the great handbooks, from Pohle to Hettinger, and the aids to clerical study. For students of theology, it is both a definition of the field and a map of its growth across the centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doxology:
A doxology is a short verse praising God, most often opening with the Greek word for glory. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces the habit of closing a rite or hymn with such a formula to the synagogue. Saint Paul uses doxologies constantly in his letters, and the earliest Christian forms address God the Father alone, or the Father through the Son, or with the Holy Spirit. The baptismal form named the three persons in parallel order.

In the fourth century the wording became a weapon against Arian teaching, since heretics leaned on the little prepositions through, in, and with. Basil defended the Church's phrasing, and the entry follows the doxology from synagogue to Mass. It closes with liturgists from Bona to Thalhofer who charted its growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistemology:
Epistemology is the branch of philosophy concerned with the value of human knowledge, from the Greek words for knowledge and discourse. The name is recent, but since Ferrier's Institutes of Metaphysics in 1854 it has come into common use, replacing terms such as applied logic, critical logic, and initial philosophy. Latin textbooks and the Louvain school call the same field criteriology.

Its exact province is still unsettled, since the Greek word for knowledge bears two senses. In the wider sense epistemology is the theory of the origin, nature, and limits of knowledge, the usual English meaning, matching the German theory of knowing. In the narrower sense it is the philosophy of the sciences: a critical study of each science's principles, hypotheses, and results, judging their logical origin, value, and objective import. Italian and French usage agrees with the narrower sense. This entry follows the wider, English meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eschatology:
Eschatology is the branch of systematic theology dealing with the doctrines of the last things, ta eschata. The Greek title is recent, but it has largely replaced the Latin De Novissimis. Other doctrines in this field are treated under their own titles, so this article merely surveys the whole field. It indicates eschatology's place in religion and compares its content across religions, illustrating the superiority of Christian teaching.

A distinction is made between the eschatology of the individual and that of the race and universe. The former, starting from personal immortality, seeks the fate of individual souls and how far the future depends on the present life. The latter deals with the resurrection and general judgment, and with the signs preceding those events. Both aspects belong to the full concept, but only Christian teaching gives both due recognition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-chron:
General Chronology, the science of fixing dates in the stream of time, is history's answer to geography's latitude and longitude. Its first need is an era, a fixed point from which all other years take their distance. The article treats the systems that matter for Christian history, from the Christian era itself to regnal years, indictions, and the reform of the calendar.

Dionysius Exiguus, a Scythian monk at Rome, framed the Christian era about 527, counting from Rome's year 753 as the birth year of Christ, with no year zero between BC and AD. Italy took it first, England early through Roman missionaries, Gaul in the eighth century, and Europe at large only after 1000. Greek Olympiads, the Julian period, and other eras fill out the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-in-the:
The Gospel in the Liturgy is an article on the public reading of Scripture in worship, inherited from the synagogue service. Before the bread and wine were brought for offering, the Liturgy of the Catechumens offered prayers, litanies, hymns, and readings to instruct the people. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the Gospel's rise to the crown of the readings.

Books were rare and few could read. What early Christians knew of the Bible, Paul's theology, and the Lord's life came from lessons heard in church and the homilies that explained them. Justin Martyr, who died about 167, describes Sunday readings of the Apostles' memoirs or the Prophets, read as long as time allowed, then exhortation by the president. Common practice read first the Prophecy, then the Epistle, and last the Gospel, as fulfillment of all the rest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heortology: Heortology, from the Greek words for festival and discourse, is the science of sacred festivals. It treats their origin, significance, and historical development in relation to epochs and incidents of the Christian year. Though the word etymologically covers feasts in general, the entry uses it specifically for the study of Christian festivals and their meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-do:
This vast article traces how Catholic dogmatic theology grew, not by single nations or men, but by the combined efforts of all nations and theologians of every century. Like the church itself, theology must stay international, the entry insists, and no national stamp fits its character. Its history falls into three periods: patristic, medieval, and modern.

The patristic age, about AD 100 to 800, honoured the great Fathers as the church's principal theologians, praised for purity of faith, holiness of life, and fullness of wisdom. Tertullian and Origen strayed on some points, and even Cyprian and Gregory of Nyssa erred on single questions. Medieval schools then carried the work forward through fierce debates, and modern theology inherited both their gains and their divisions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hymnody-and-h:
Hymnody, from the Greek for hymn song, covers hymnal verse or religious lyric, including both hymn-singer and hymn-poet. Hymnology is the science of hymnody: the historical, philological, and aesthetic study of hymns and hymn writers. Hymnology is still recent in origin, and the vast Latin hymn material long lay buried in Europe's library manuscripts.

Interest in spreading knowledge and love of hymns, especially Latin hymns, dates to the twelfth century, and research quickened in England, France, and Germany from the mid-nineteenth century. Yet a German encyclopedia judged that research into Latin church poetry had made little progress despite nineteenth-century studies. Even the compilations of Neale, Mone, and Daniel, once thought fairly complete, proved only a beginning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lessons-in-th:
Lessons in the Liturgy, apart from the Gospel, traces Bible, Martyrs' Acts, and Fathers' lessons as a key part of worship in every rite from the start.  The Christian synaxis copied the synagogue service: lessons, psalm-singing, homilies, and prayers. Christians read their own Scriptures too: Gospels and Apostles' letters.

St. Paul bids the Thessalonians have his letter read to all the brethren. He tells the Colossians to exchange letters with Laodicea for reading. The common view that Paul's Gospel through all the churches meant Luke's Gospel read in assemblies shows the same.  Tertullian says Rome joined Law and Prophets with Gospels and Apostolic letters in public reading. At first Acts of Martyrs, letters, homilies of leading bishops, and other edifying writings were also read aloud.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgy:
Liturgy, from a Greek word for public duty, is the Church's official public worship, set against private prayer. At Athens rich citizens bore a leitourgia at their own cost, funding choruses, banquets, or warships, and the Septuagint took the word for temple service.

Christians kept the religious sense, and the entry uses it to compare all the great rites: Alexandrine, Ambrosian, Antiochene, Celtic, Gallican, Mozarabic, Sarum, Syrian, and more. It asks how fixed forms grew out of free prayer in the early Church, and how sister rites split, borrowed, and kept a family likeness across East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrology:
A martyrology is a list of martyrs and saints set out by feast day, that is, by calendar. Since martyr commemorations began, each church kept its own list, and local lists grew by borrowing neighbours' names. When the martyr era closed, those famed for holy life and ascetic practice joined the lists. Rome's mid-fourth-century martyrology, or ferial, survives in two lists, Depositio martyrum and Depositio episcoporum, usually found united elsewhere.

The Hieronymian Martyrology and its kin show hasty work, while historical martyrologies link to great Greek synaxaries, a key counterpart. Critical study stays hard, given the sheer mix of elements involved. For long, study of the Hieronymian text yielded few results.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mental-pathol:
Mental pathology is surveyed under five heads. They are where mental powers sit in the brain, what disturbs them, the kinds of insanity, freedom of the will and responsibility, and pathological changes in brain structure. The kinds alone run to fourteen. They are melancholia and mania, general paresis, juvenile insanity, senile dementia, chronic delusion, alcoholic disease, epileptic psychosis, hysterical psychosis, imbecility, compulsive ideas, menstrual psychosis, impulsive psychosis, and sexual psychopathy.

On localization, the cerebral cortex, the thin coat over the brain's whole surface, holds areas linked by long nerve tracts to sense organs, skin, and muscles. These form the Projection System. Other areas, tied to no outer world but joined closely to each other and to the projection areas, form the Association System. In the first, elementary functions sit in sharp centres for limb movements, taste, hearing, sight, and more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-theolog:
Moral theology is the branch of theology that studies how human beings should act in light of God's revelation. It stands apart from dogmatic theology, which studies what is to be believed. Theology itself divides into natural theology, what reason alone can reach about God, and supernatural theology, the science of God and divine things known through revelation. That science includes his works of salvation and our guidance toward him.

Faith gives believers these truths in outline, but science demands they be deepened, defended by reasons and arranged in order. Moral theology does that work for conduct. The entry surveys its history from Scripture and the Fathers through Aquinas and later schools. It covers its sources in law, conscience and virtue, and its method for judging concrete acts, sins and duties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-theo:
Mystical theology is the science of acts, experiences and states of the soul that human effort cannot produce, even with the ordinary aid of divine grace. It covers extraordinary prayer, higher contemplation in all its varieties and grades, private revelations, visions, and the union growing from these between God and the soul, known as the mystical union.

As the science of all that is extraordinary between Divinity and the human spirit, it complements ascetical theology, which treats Christian perfection gained by practising virtue and observing the counsels. Its contents are doctrinal as well as experimental. It records the experiences of mystically favoured souls and lays down rules for their guidance, drawn from Scripture, the Fathers and theologian-mystics. Its precepts serve directors of souls, guarding them from error while easing their advance, and it notes false systems such as Quietism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ontology:
Ontology, from Greek words for being and science, is the first branch of metaphysics, the philosophy of being itself. Aristotle called it first philosophy, theology, and wisdom, Clauberg used ontology in its literal sense, and Wolff fixed it as general metaphysics against cosmology, psychology, and theodicy.

Its matter runs from the concept of being in widest range, through essence and existence, act and potency, to principles like contradiction and identity. Then come properties as wide as being itself: unity, truth, and goodness, with order and beauty beside them, and the split of being into finite and infinite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palaeontology:
Palaeontology, the science of fossils, treats extinct animals and plants of long ago. It covers their features, sorting, life and habits, spread across the earth, and order in time. It also draws lessons from them for the history of living things and of the earth itself. It stands close to geology, botany, zoology, comparative anatomy, and embryology, which serve it as helper sciences.

Fossil plants form palaeophytology, fossil animals palaeozoology. Even in antiquity, sea fossils inland led thinkers like Xenophanes, Strabo, and Seneca to infer a changed layout of sea and land. Medieval writers mostly called fossils sports of earth's shaping power. Later pages trace the science's rise, its use in dating rock layers, and its bearing on descent theory, where fossil series of small steps are weighed against gaps in the record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pastoral-theo:
Pastoral theology treats the care of souls as a science, and this entry defines it, relates it to other theological sciences, and traces its history, sources, and contents. It belongs to practical theology. Every branch of theology aims to make priests ministers of Christ and dispensers of God's mysteries. Pastoral theology takes the findings of dogmatic, moral, juridical, ascetical, liturgical, and exegetical study, and applies them to priestly ministry.

Dogmatic theology sets out the Church as keeper of revealed truth, and pastoral theology teaches the priest his share in handing it down. Moral theology states God's and the Church's laws, means of grace, and hindrances, and pastoral theology shows their bearing on a priest's life, alone and among his people. Canon law gathers church laws, and pastoral theology applies them, with later pages on preaching, catechism, confession, and sick calls. Its lessons reach the priest in pulpit, confessional, and sickroom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrology:
Patrology is the study of the Fathers' writings, more often called patristics or patristic study in England. Some German writers split the field. Fessler defines patrology as the science that equips readers to use the Fathers. It weighs their authority, tests of genuineness, difficulties, and rules of use. Patristics, by contrast, gathers all on faith, morals, or discipline from their writings. Literary history, a third science, tells the Fathers' lives and works.

Those distinctions are little observed and seem needless, since they are only facets of patristic study within fundamental theology, positive theology, and literary history. Patrology also takes its name from Migne's great collections, the Latin Patrology in 221 volumes and the Greek in 161. Bardenhewer's handbook, translated by Shahan, stands as the most serviceable guide of its kind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pax-in-the-li:
Pax vobis, or vobiscum, is a liturgical greeting of Scriptural origin, like Dominus vobiscum. The Gospels give may your peace come, may your peace return to you, peace to this house, and peace to you. Grace and peace opens epistles of Saint Paul and Saint Peter, and Saint John's letters and the Apocalypse. Our Lord and the Apostles quoted it from the Old Testament, and it survived in liturgy and inscriptions as a memorial of apostolic times.

Like Dominus vobiscum, bishops first used it in liturgy, as Pax vobis, greeting the faithful at Mass's start before the Collect. When Confiteor, Introit, and Gloria were later added, Pax vobis or Dominus vobiscum stayed. Now bishops and prelates alone use Pax vobis at the first Collect, priests using Dominus vobiscum. Hence Dominus vobiscum became the usual lead-in to orations and most prayers, while Greeks kept Pax omnibus or Pax vobiscum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psychology:
Psychology, from the Greek words for soul and study, is the science of the soul and its workings. This long encyclopedia entry notes a shift in the word's use: over the past century it has come to mean the science of mental phenomena, the processes and states of human consciousness. Research has split into distinct fields, each claiming the rank of a separate science. The term itself appeared near the end of the sixteenth century, in Goclenius in 1590 and Casmann's work of 1594.

Higher mental life poses the entry's central problem. Explaining the loftier products of consciousness seems impossible without some metaphysical view of the mind and its link to reality. Dewey's warning is quoted: views about the mind's nature show on almost every page. A neo-Scholastic bibliography, with Baldwin's dictionary and Eisler's lexicon, closes a survey that maps a young science still arguing about its own foundations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scriptural-tr:
Scriptural tropology is the theory and practice of reading the figurative meaning of Holy Writ. The literal meaning, the meaning God intended the words to carry, may itself be figurative or plain. In the Song of Songs, for instance, the inspired meaning is always figurative. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia distinguishes two layers of inspired sense.

The typical meaning is the inspired meaning of words about Old Testament persons, things, and actions that serve as types, or foreshadowings, of New Testament persons, things, and actions. Tropology studies how such figures work, and the entry, cross-referring to exegesis, gives readers a compact key to a way of reading that shaped medieval preaching and commentary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-secular-clerg: Priests who live and work in the wider world, rather than under a religious rule inside a monastery, are known as the secular clergy. This short entry sets them beside the regular clergy. Regular clergy follow a rule and give up personal property. The secular priest keeps his own goods instead. He owes his bishop obedience in church law. He shares the celibacy of ordained life without taking a religious vow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-slavonic-lang:
Slavonic ranks next to Latin among church languages. Unlike Greek or Latin, which each serve a single rite, it serves both the Greek and Roman rites. In Byzantine form it reaches 115,000,000 people, Catholic and Orthodox, while in Roman form it serves 100,000 Catholics along the Adriatic in Dalmatia and lower Croatia. Cyril and Methodius translated the Byzantine liturgy and offices from Greek into Old Slavonic about 866.

Cyril devised the Cyrillic alphabet for Slavonic sounds as spoken by Bulgars and Moravians. Methodius translated the whole Bible into Slavonic. Summoned to Rome in 868, the brothers won Adrian II's approval for their Slavonic liturgy. An older Glagolitic alphabet, linked by tradition to Jerome, still survives along the Adriatic highlands. A casual hearer could not tell a Slavonic priest from a Latin one except by the language spoken aloud.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sociology:
Sociology's claim to a place among the sciences draws varied dispute, this entry says. Some deny it any distinct problem beyond the accepted social sciences, while others grant its future prospects but fault its present state. Popular confusion worsens matters, mixing sociology with charity, reform, statistics, socialism, sanitation, criminology, and politics. Yet the young science has won university recognition and deeply affected nearby sciences.

Its method is mainly inductive, drawing on ethnology, comparison, statistics, and the study of mind, while its core problem is finding and explaining patterns among social facts. The sociologist seeks a whole view of movements such as democracy, liberty, war, tariffs, labour organization, and class conflict, tracing their wider bearings and place within social processes. Deductive system-building has not yet produced undisputed results.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teleology:
Teleology, from Greek telos, end, and logos, science, is seldom used for the branch of philosophy dealing with ends or final causes. It usually means the doctrine that design, purpose, or finality exists in the world. Effects are in some manner intentional, and no complete account of the universe is possible without final causes. With mechanism, it admits determined efficient causes and the search for laws.

Against mechanism, it claims that laws and efficient causes reveal a directive principle and finality in nature. The question is not whether man sees because he has eyes or has eyes in order to see. Final and efficient causes are not mutually exclusive. Any result follows an unbroken chain of active causes, and final cause explains how that activity is directed toward useful results. Nor must it name every end, any more than mechanism must name every cause.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-alexandri:
Egypt's ancient pattern of worship takes centre stage here, traced back by tradition to Mark the Evangelist, first bishop of Alexandria. From that parent rite, the entry explains, grew three families still in use across the old patriarchate. They were the Greek Liturgy of Saint Mark, Coptic versions drawn from it, and Ethiopian uses built on the Liturgy of the Twelve Apostles.

By setting these rites side by side, scholars can partly rebuild the worship of Alexandria before the split over Monophysite teaching and the Council of Chalcedon in 451. Early witnesses such as Clement, Athanasius, Serapion, and Pseudo-Dionysius supply further clues. The entry walks through the Mass of the Catechumens and the Mass of the Faithful, from readings and psalms to the kiss of peace and the Eucharistic prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-cross-and:
Cross in worship, as object, gesture, feast, and sign, fills this wide liturgical entry under eight heads. Material objects open it. The altar cross is hardly traceable before the thirteenth century, despite Tours's canon of 567, which likely meant Host particles laid crosswise on the corporal, not a cross standing on the altar. Innocent III's treatise on the Mass shows the newer custom.

Liturgical forms, feasts of the Holy Cross, rite of Adoration, manual sign of blessing, church dedications, orders and crusades, and the cross outside Catholicism follow in turn. Processional crosses, pectoral crosses, and blessings with the cross reveal a symbol woven into every hour of Catholic prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-law-of-co:
Modern physics meets theism in this long philosophical entry, centred on the Law of Conservation of Energy. Critics have pressed it against miracles, free will, and the soul's immateriality, creation, and immortality, and the entry answers as fully as space allows. Energy, from Greek energeia or operation, means in science the capacity of an agent for doing work.

Work means producing motion against resistance. Energy appears in two states: kinetic, or energy of motion, and potential, or energy of position. From these definitions the entry builds its case, testing whether a fixed total of energy truly shuts out divine action or leaves room for a soul that acts without adding force.
chess-strategy:

The boards are drawn in plain text characters, with a key explaining the letters used for rook, knight, bishop, queen, king, and pawn.

Two parts organize the teaching, each with its own chapters and prefaces from author and translator. Readers who find the text diagrams hard to read are advised to set positions up on a real board with actual pieces. The approach suits patient students: learn how pieces work together, how pawns shape a position, and how a small edge grows into a win. Lasker, a master player, writes as a teacher first.
criminal-sociology:

Ferri argues that crime grows from bodily, mental, and social causes working together. One part surveys criminal anthropology, meaning the study of the criminal's body and mind, from skulls and faces to heredity and moral feeling.

Later parts sort criminals into classes: born criminals, habitual criminals, occasional criminals, criminals of passion, and the insane. Statistics on crime rates support the scheme. Ferri wanted punishment fitted to the type of offender, with prevention ranked above revenge. Modern readers will find some claims dated, but the book shaped how Europe debated crime.

govdocs-archive_org-nciplesOfTopological:
Kurt Lewin, the Gestalt psychologist who founded much of modern social psychology, published Principles of Topological Psychology with McGraw-Hill in 1936. The book sets out his field theory, the idea that behavior is a function of the person and their environment taken together.

Lewin maps what he calls the life space, the whole situation as a person experiences it, using ideas from topology to draw its regions, paths, and barriers. The method was his attempt to give psychology scientific rigor without losing the wholeness Gestalt theory prized. The book remains a landmark of social psychology.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
The International Atomic Energy Agency, the world's nuclear watchdog, came into existence in 1956 and 1957. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in October 2017 for its sixtieth anniversary. The agency was born despite complete skepticism from the Soviet Union.

India and other countries fought sharply over whether inspections would be equitable. The United States insisted that an American head the new organization. Those founding arguments, over fairness and control, still shape the agency's work. The documents show an institution designed amid distrust, which may explain why its inspection system was built to survive disagreement rather than assume goodwill.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Repor: The Office of Technology Assessment was Congress's own science adviser from 1972 until lawmakers abolished it in 1995, producing hundreds of studies on everything from missile defense to medical care. music-notation-and-terminology:

Gehrkens wrote for school music teachers and their classes. Terms are defined in plain order, with figures to show each point. The text even thanks helpers for a figured bass example. nasa-tm-19690008664-photodisintegration-:
F. W. Stecker, of the Theoretical Studies Branch at Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this December 1968 preprint, X-641-68-480. He studies photodisintegration: atomic nuclei flying at ultrahigh energy, broken apart by light that fills all of space. Such cosmic ray nuclei cross vast distances before reaching Earth, and the universal radiation field attacks them the whole way.

Stecker calculates in detail how effective that breakup process really is. He concludes it cannot explain the air shower observations at the highest energies by itself. One escape remains, he notes: a large flow of infrared light between the galaxies, which may recently have been detected. The paper closes by discussing what else its results imply for cosmic ray origins.
nasa-tm-19710007275-calibration-of-the-n:
H. Whiteside of Federal City College and C. J. Crannell and H. Crannell of Catholic University joined J. F. Ormes and M. J. Ryan of Goddard on this report. It is a preliminary report, dated January 1971. It covers the calibration of Goddard's high energy cosmic ray experiment.

The instrument was checked against a test beam at Brookhaven National Laboratory. The report describes the conditions under which that calibration ran. nasa-tm-19710008961-space-shuttle-avioni: Space Shuttle Avionics Technology is the title of a NASA technical memorandum on the electronic control and guidance systems planned for the space shuttle. nasa-tm-19720016318-useful-new-technolog:
Useful New Technology is a NASA booklet explaining the Technology Utilization Program. Space research produced far more than rockets and moonshots. New materials, tools, and methods spilled into ordinary life. The program existed to spread those advances widely. Its stated aim was a better return on the public's space investment. Industry, schools, hospitals, and cities were all invited to draw on the results. The booklet tells readers how to take part.

Chapters cover the industrial benefits already gained from space work. They explain how to obtain NASA technical data for a problem. nassau-bantu-sociology:
Robert Hamill Nassau distilled forty years in Gabon into Bantu Sociology in 1914. The missionary knew West African life from the inside, not from books. Kinship, law, marriage, and custom stand as his main subjects here.

Nassau shows how clan ties order birth, work, worship, and death. He treats Bantu custom as a full system, worthy of respect. His long residence gives each rule a human face and story. The book pairs with his Fetichism in West Africa in the catalog. Missionary records at their most humane and detailed fill these careful pages. Nassau judges custom by its inner logic, not by foreign scorn.
on-the-study-of-zoology:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this lecture on studying zoology. He begins with the old, wide sense of natural history. Linnaeus covered minerals, plants, and animals in one system. No single scholar could repeat that feat now, Huxley says. Knowledge has grown too vast for one mind.

Zoology and botany have grown closer together, he argues. Both now sit under the common head of biology. Mineralogy has drifted away from its old partners. Students must choose animals or plants and specialize. Broad laws still link the living kingdoms, he notes. Huxley urges learning from living animals directly.

siouan-sociology:

Two years among the Ponka grounded Dorsey in their tongue and kindred dialects. He gathered rich stores on arts, customs, traditions, and beliefs. Illness drove him home in 1873, yet study went on. His record preserves how Siouan peoples ordered kin, camp, and ceremony.
